A.explanation: This is about 100 times too small and comes from mishandling the $\text{cm s}^{-1}$ to $\text{m s}^{-1}$ conversion when finding acceleration.

B.explanation: This is close but uses a rounded acceleration of $0.30 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ if the $30 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ initial velocity is ignored.

D.explanation: This is about 10 times too large and comes from using the velocity change in $\text{cm s}^{-1}$ directly as if it were in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

hints: Look at the velocity-time graph: it starts at $30 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ at $0 \text{ s}$ and reaches $150 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ at $5.0 \text{ s}$, so find the change in velocity.
Recall that the gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration, and the resultant force links to acceleration by $F = ma$.
Convert the $120 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ increase to $1.20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ before dividing by $5.0 \text{ s}$, then use $m = F/a$ with $F = 300 \text{ N}$.
walkthrough: Read the graph values: initial velocity $u = 30 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ and final velocity $v = 150 \text{ cm s}^{-1}$ at $t = 5.0 \text{ s}$.
Find the change in velocity: $\Delta v = 150 - 30 = 120 \text{ cm s}^{-1} = 1.20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Calculate acceleration from the gradient: $a = \Delta v / \Delta t = 1.20/5.0 = 0.24 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Use Newton's second law for the constant resultant force: $F = ma$, so $m = F/a$.
Substitute $F = 300 \text{ N}$: $m = 300/0.24 = 1250 \text{ kg}$, which to two significant figures is about $1300 \text{ kg}$. This is option C.
